content.thinking:
I need to write the whole file carefully in one pass to avoid type or runtime errors. I'm planning out the pixel art dungeon props: a flagstone floor slab, a wooden chest with iron bands and an open lid showing coins, standing torch sconces, barrels, and a pile of bones with a skull.

Now I'm thinking through the joint structure for the builder — a root joint for the base, plus a hinge joint for the chest lid, since plain objects need a root but moving parts like the lid require their own joint. I'm also sketching out realistic sizing: the chest around 0.9m wide and 0.55m tall, barrels about 0.8m tall, torches roughly 1.6m tall.

I'm figuring out how the base floor slab sits at y=0 with everything resting on top, and planning the pixel-art texture approach using a small texel size so surfaces stay crisp without smoothing. I'm working out what textures I'll need, starting with a stone tile for the flagstone floor and considering whether to build the floor from individual tileBox flagstones instead of one large texture.

I'm settling on a single procedurally-drawn flagstone pattern baked into a 128x96 pixel texture, with a deterministic noise pattern for mortar lines and shading, covering the floor in one piece. I'm also planning to keep the number of flat solid colors used across parts under the 64-color limit, since textures don't count against that cap.

Now I'm sketching helper functions for creating a tiled box part and setting up the base joint, including how rotation and texture color handling will work for each piece.

With that groundwork set, I'm starting to lay out the actual scene: a 3.2 by 2.4 floor centered at the origin, and placing props like a chest near the front-left, figuring out their positions and facing directions.

The chest itself needs a body and a hinged lid opened about 100 degrees to reveal gold coins inside, and I'm wrestling with how to handle its rotation—since parts only take world placements, it's simpler to keep the chest axis-aligned rather than computing a rotation transform around its center.

I decide the lid rotation should be handled with a pose call on the hinge joint instead, building the lid closed first then rotating it about the X axis. Working out the trigonometry for which direction lifts the front open, I conclude the angle needs to be negative, roughly -105 degrees.

Still building the lid extrude geometry...

Computing lid column spans...

Figuring out band dimensions...

There's some drift between the band and lid alignment at various columns since the band cells are slightly bigger than the lid cells, which could let the lid poke out past the band edges in spots. I think the simpler fix is to just make the band one cell taller everywhere using the same cell size as the lid, with matching z-offsets, rather than trying to track the drift precisely.

Actually simpler to just match band columns to lid's exact column range rather than adding extra ones, letting it protrude only 0.02 above the lid to avoid z-fighting on coplanar faces. If the front/back faces end up coincident with the lid's, I may need to extend the band one column past each side so the overlapping faces don't fight.

So band heights at edges equal lid height plus one, matching the lid's silhouette offset outward by a cell everywhere except the bottom, which sits coplanar with the body top and should stay hidden by back-face culling. I'm checking that this coincident bottom-top pairing won't z-fight since one faces down and the other up, though I need to watch what happens once the lid opens and the underside becomes visible.

Now I'm sketching out the chest's actual geometry: a solid open box with four walls and a floor so the interior is visible when the lid lifts, with a coin pile inside. I'm working out dimensions—body outer width, depth, height, wall thickness, floor position, hinge placement at the back edge, and reconciling the lid's column count and texel size against the body's depth so the panel proportions line up with the plank texture tiling.

Defining seam rules per axis...

Checking texel density against painted area (roughly 20 m²) gives about 7.6 texels per cell at 2048, which is plenty crisp; considering whether to drop to 1024 if the painted region ends up small, but 2048 should stay safe even sharing a 4096 atlas.

Deciding what gets textured versus painted: tileBoxes carry textures for most surfaces, while cellPaint handles rounded or irregular things like barrels, bones, and torches. For barrels I'm using a lathe shape with 10-12 segments, blocky stave profile with a bulge, and deriving stave seams from the angle value in the lathe's parameter array.

For stave seams, I need the angle relative to the barrel's center rather than the texel's own coordinate, so I'll compute it via atan2 against a barrel center and feed that into a dedicated barrelPaint factory function. With 12 staves at roughly 8 cells each, a single-cell-wide dark seam gives a clean plank look, and for the metal hoops I'm considering whether to paint flat bands or build them as actual bulging lathe rings for a more three-dimensional effect.

Still writing lathe profile...

I'm also planning variety across the three barrels: one closed standing, one open with dark liquid inside, and one tipped on its side using a horizontal lathe axis, plus a separate textured disc for the top lid.

For the tipped barrel I need to generalize the stave-paint function to work with an arbitrary axis direction rather than assuming vertical, computing perpendicular basis vectors from the axis to get the angle around it, and I'll place hoops along that same axis for consistency.

I'll keep the barrel intact but add a leaking puddle near the open end, plus small wedge chocks to hold it steady. I could also add a stenciled label or chalk marking on the front using a thin textured plane for detail.

Working through placing the label plane correctly against the barrel's curved surface, accounting for the lathe polygon's radius so it sits flush rather than floating.

Instead I'll use a proper decal projected onto the barrel part's surface, which handles the curvature automatically. Now I'm sketching out the full component list for the scene, starting with the floor flagstone tile.

For the floor, I'm considering a stone slab with cracks and moss patches rendered as thin flat boxes, plus some scattered pebbles for rubble. I'm weighing whether to add cobwebs or a broken wall chunk for atmosphere, but deciding the torches can stand freely without extra wall dressing since the scene should stay focused.

For the torches themselves, I'm designing two standing posts about 1.5m tall: a square stone plinth base, an iron pole, and a bracket cup holding a cloth-wrapped torch head. The fire is built from crossed pixel-textured flame planes with a glow effect, using double-sided cards positioned upward from the bracket.

I'm also adding tiny glowing ember sparks around each torch, and considering a floor decal beneath each one — a pixelated radial dither pattern in warm orange tones to simulate light spilling onto the ground.

Now thinking through the spike trap design: a sunken pit with a stone border frame sitting on the floor, with a dark interior plate showing a grid of holes for spikes, and iron spike cones that extend up from those holes.

Working out the spike geometry and coloring...

I'm also thinking about adding a bloody skeleton victim impaled on the spikes for narrative detail—bones like skull, ribcage, and scattered long bones placed near the trap to tell a story.

Now I'm working out how to build bones from simple shapes: rods for the shafts with knob ends, using a small-scale cell-paint shading function to color them procedurally based on surface normal and noise, picking from a bone color ramp at a fine resolution appropriate for such small parts.

Checking that this paint resolution holds up across the whole scene: at roughly 10 square meters of painted surface (barrels, hoops, lid, torches) the texel density comfortably supports a 0.01m cell size with crisp edges, so it should look fine without needing to paint the floor. Now I'm sketching the skull as a box-based cranium around 0.17 by 0.14 by 0.17 meters.

Planning the skulls as pixel-textured boxes: a cranium box with a front face painted with eye sockets and nose, and a separate smaller jaw box below with teeth drawn in, using a simple skin layout scaled to the right dimensions. I'm working out rotation order so that tilting happens locally before yaw is applied, letting skulls rest naturally on their side or face a direction, with the jaw treated as its own static part slightly below rather than an animated joint. Next I'm thinking through how to build the ribcage using curved sweeps along catmull curves for each rib.

I'm sizing the ribcage to roughly 0.3 wide, 0.2-0.25 tall, with 7 ribs spaced along the spine, scaling bone thickness a bit chunkier than realistic for stylization. For the spine I'm laying out a row of small vertebra boxes continuing from the ribcage into a tail toward the pelvis.

To cut down part count, I'm merging same-colored bone geometries using BufferGeometryUtils' mergeGeometries, applying transform matrices to each box before merging so vertebrae and other bones combine into single draw calls while still painting correctly from model-space position and normal data. For femurs and other long bones I'm generating a simple rod geometry.

Setting femur at 0.38 long with thin shaft and small knobs at the ends, one offset for the bent femoral head. For the full skeleton I'm planning roughly three femurs/tibias, two arm bones, a ribcage built from arched sweeps, and a pelvis made from a stepped extrusion.

I'm also adding duplicate skulls, loose ribs, scattered vertebrae, and tiny finger boxes for detail. Near the skeleton I'm placing a short iron shackle made of a few torus rings lying flat and linked together to suggest a chain. Inside the chest I'm layering gold-colored boxes into a coin-heap pattern with small glowing gem cubes mixed in.

Adding scattered coins and glow settings...

Now I'm planning the chest's hardware details: iron corner brackets, a front lock plate with keyhole texture and gold ring, vertical iron straps with rivets on the body front, ring handles on the sides, and feet at the base.

Right, cell paint gets baked at build-time position, so painting before posing is correct. For the lid joint, I'm setting it up as a hinge at the hinge point with no explicit aim, so it inherits the parent's orientation, then rotating it about the x-axis during pose.

For bone direction, I'll point dir along [0,0,1] for the lid's depth axis, making local X the hinge roll axis — that should work fine for the side determination too. For parts without an explicit bone assignment, they'll snap to the nearest bone segment, so anything near the chest likely binds to the base-to-lid segment rather than the lid itself.

To avoid ambiguity, I should always pass `bone: base` explicitly in helper functions for every part that isn't on the lid, since explicit bone wins over nearest-segment defaults. Lid-specific parts get `bone: lid`, and I'll apply this bone option consistently across spike, rod, sweep, extrude, lathe, card, and decal helpers.

Now I'm defining color ramps for textures using a palette-snapping helper, starting with a cool purple-grey stone ramp and moving on to a wood ramp.

Writing more color ramps...

Still defining color ramps...

Now I'm writing a hash-based pixel randomness function for texture generation, then planning out the floor tile layout with stone rows at a 128x96 resolution.

I'm sizing flagstone rows at 16px (0.48m) with randomized stone widths, mortar lines, bevel shading, and speckle noise. Drawing stone rows...

I realize there's a wrapping issue at the tile edges—stones that extend past x=128 wrap around and overwrite the beginning pixels, conflicting with the first stone. I should just clamp and skip off-grid pixels instead of wrapping, to keep the tiling clean.

For the mortar lines, I'm drawing the darkest color at yy===0 or xx===0, adding a few random cracked pixels, and scattering mossy pixels near mortar with low probability for texture variation. The slab side faces will just show a cropped slice of the tile texture near the top rows (mortar lines), which should still look reasonably like stone edges, so I'll accept that as-is.

Now I'm planning the floor's physical layout at 3.4 by 2.6 units, placing torches, barrels, a chest, a spike trap, and bones across the back and front corners of the scene to form a believable dungeon composition.

I need to double-check the trap's footprint boundaries against the tipped barrel's position so they don't overlap — adjusting the barrel's z-position slightly back and shifting the trap's center to keep clearance between them.

Now I'm figuring out where to place the skeleton remains, since the gap next to the chest and trap is too narrow. I'll enlarge the floor to 3.6 by 2.8, re-center the trap at roughly (0.95, 0.35), and lay the skeleton along the x-axis near the front-center of the scene instead.

I'll extend one spike with a skull impaled on top, plus a hanging rib for extra detail. For the floor and torches, I'm setting the room extents to roughly ±1.8 by ±1.4, placing torches at x=±1.5, z=-1.0, with a total height around 1.65 so they remain the tallest feature. Now I'm designing the torch itself as an iron standing fixture with a stepped stone plinth base.

Still working out the torch geometry...

Checking the full point sequence confirms the shape doesn't self-intersect, so the polygon works cleanly with 8 segments using the iron cell color. Now I'm sketching the torch head: a wooden stick fitting inside the cup, topped with a wrapped cloth-and-pitch bundle, dark pitch with possibly a reddish cloth accent.

Adding flame layers and ember glow...

Also sketching a stippled light pool for the floor beneath the torch using a dithered radial pattern, so the firelight reads as scattered orange pixels fading against the dark ground.

Now moving to the spike trap, I'm placing its frame around center (0.95, 0.35), checking that its bounding box doesn't collide with the torches positioned elsewhere in the scene.

I'm detailing its components: a stone outer frame with carved bevel edges and iron corner studs, plus a recessed iron pit plate with an engraved grid-of-holes texture at the trap's center.

Now I'm placing 25 retractable spikes in a 5×5 grid across the plate, varying their extended lengths for a worn, randomized look, with iron collars ringing each hole and a blood-stained, rusted finish painted onto the plate texture for grime detail. For the spike geometry, I'm using a pyramid-like shape with four sides, and planning to merge the repeated collar and spike meshes efficiently rather than creating 25 separate objects.

I'm now writing a procedural wood plank texture generator, drawing horizontal rows of planks with randomized tones, seam highlights, nail marks, and grain streaks to make the chest surface look weathered.

Working out plank boundary randomization and face dimensions relative to tile size, then considering wall thickness for the chest body geometry—thin faces around 2.5 texels need careful handling.

Now I'm computing the chest body box dimensions: setting width, depth, height and wall thickness, then deriving the floor box, front/back wall, and side wall positions as axis-aligned boxes relative to the center point.

For the interior, I'm skipping a lining layer since the gold coin heap will cover it, and instead stacking tapered heap layers (gold tile boxes shrinking in width/depth as they rise) to get the top heap height sitting below the rim so it's visible when the lid is open from above.

I'm also adding small glowing gem boxes (ruby, sapphire, emerald) scattered on the heap, plus a small gold chalice sitting on top using a lathe shape with flat gold cell-paint shading instead of glow, and I'm planning iron reinforcement bands across the lid's stepped profile.

Now I'm working out the lid's height profile using a sine-based curve so it rises from thin edges to a taller center, forming a pixel-stepped dome rather than a sharp vertical front face.

I'm deciding the lid doesn't need visible interior detail since nothing will be shown inside when opened, so I'll skip adding lining and just focus on positioning the lid extrusion correctly relative to the chest's depth and origin.

Working through the band placement, I'm figuring out that the thickness direction is centered symmetrically along x, with lid width slightly larger than the body (0.94 vs 0.92), and realizing the decorative bands only wrap the top and front/back faces, not the lid's side faces, so they need to sit at offset x positions around ±0.34.

At the ends I need to add wrapped end-bands near the lid tips (x≈±0.47), but if the band's end face sits exactly coplanar with the lid's end face, they'll z-fight—so I'm nudging the band center outward slightly (e.g. center 0.44, width 0.07) so it protrudes just a touch past the lid face and avoids the overlap.

Now I'm placing the hasp and lock hardware: a lock plate box on the body's front near the top rim, and a hasp plate on the lid's front face positioned to bridge down toward the lock, sizing both pieces (roughly 0.07–0.12 wide, ~0.11–0.15 tall, 0.015–0.02 thick) and offsetting them slightly outward from the front z-face so they read as applied ironwork rather than fused into the surface.

Then I'm adding corner hardware and straps: four vertical iron corner-post boxes (~0.065–0.07 wide, 0.4 tall) at each chest corner using a riveted iron tile texture at a fine texel scale, plus two front vertical straps (about 0.07 wide, 0.34 tall, thin) positioned symmetrically on either side of center to reinforce the front face visually.

For handles, I'm placing small torus rings on the sides, rotated so they face outward in the YZ plane near the top of the body, giving the chest a hanging-ring look. I'm also scattering a coin spill in front of the chest — around 18 flat merged cylinder discs (some lying flat, some tilted on edge) in two gold tones just above the floor, with additional coins scattered across the top of the heap for extra texture.

Now I'm sketching out a general barrel-building function: define a bottom point, axis direction, random seed, and whether it's open-topped, then generate the barrel body as a radial profile curve extruded along that axis (roughly 0.86 units tall, bulging in the middle and narrowing at both ends) that I can later close off at the top for sealed barrels.

Still shaping the lid profile...

For a tilted barrel, I realize the top face isn't simply axis-1 anymore, so I need a generic plank-seam rule based on projecting the point onto a perpendicular side vector relative to the barrel's actual axis direction.

For stave divisions, I'm computing an angular coordinate around the axis using two perpendicular basis vectors, then bucketing that angle into roughly 12 stave segments with seam darkening near the edges of each segment and per-stave color variation from a hash. I'm also layering in vertical grain noise and planning dirt-darkening near the top and bottom ends based on position along the axis.

For moss and wood color, I'm adding moss patches on upward-facing surfaces using noise thresholds, and picking wood ramp colors based on a tone value shaded by the surface's world-up component, with dithering enabled for a pixelated look.

Now I'm working out the hoop geometry: placing four metal hoops at specific heights along the barrel, computing the radius at each height from a profile function, and lathing a ring cross-section that bulges slightly beyond the stave surface using inner and outer radius offsets.

I'm settling on 10 staves and 10 lathe segments to keep the barrel faceted for a pixel-art look, matching hoop segments to stave count, and deciding the exact rotational phase doesn't matter since painting is cell-based rather than tied to vertex seams. For hoop coloring I'll use an iron paint ramp with rust tones, skipping rivets for simplicity, and for the open barrel variant I'm sketching a profile that curves outward then back inward near the rim to approximate wall thickness and create a visible interior.

For the interior, I'm working out the inner wall radius so it tapers down to the liquid surface at y=0.70, then adding a separate thin green-black cylinder disc there to represent the water, keeping it slightly smaller than the outer wall so the rim reads correctly.

The gap leaves a thin ring of dark wood visible like a meniscus effect, which works fine, so I'll settle on a disc radius of 0.27 for the water surface.

For color I'm thinking murky green with a sparkle dither, maybe skip extra floating debris and just add a simple wooden ladle resting across the open barrel's rim for detail.

Now I'm adding a front-facing spigot made of small iron and wood pieces, plus a decal brand of a skull-and-crossbones and a "RUM" label stamped onto the closed barrel's surface, positioning it using the barrel's front-facing coordinates.

For the tipped barrel, I'm working out its lying axis direction and bottom contact point so the belly radius determines the resting height correctly.

Positioning the puddle plane just past the open end along direction A, with a pixel-art alpha blob texture in dark green with highlights so it reads as spilled liquid without any glow, and orienting the plane to face upward and align with the barrel's tilt direction.

For the tipped barrel's open interior, I'm working out how to darken the inner wall faces by checking whether a surface normal points inward toward the axis versus outward, using the radial direction relative to tilt axis A to decide which cells get a darker shading ramp. I'm estimating the sprite will need around 350-450 parts total, and now moving on to torch details.

I'm checking for overlaps between torch plinths and barrel positions near the walls — torch A at roughly (-1.5,-1.0) was clipping into barrel1, so I'm nudging torch A to (-1.55,-1.05) and barrel1 to (-0.95,-0.55) to clear the gap, while confirming torch B at (1.55,-1.05) still fits within the floor bounds. Now I'm recalculating the tipped barrel's center and its end-cap positions along the tilt axis A to position it correctly relative to these adjusted neighbors.

Checking distances again, that spacing seems too tight, so I'm repositioning barrel2 to (-0.4,-0.62) and the tipped barrel to (0.5,-0.85), which gives enough clearance between them.

Good, that leaves a 0.06 gap in z which clears. I'm considering adding a small half-size keg on top as a fourth prop, maybe a tiny keg around 0.5 scale to fill the space.

Actually I'll check placement near the chest instead — testing a small staved wooden bucket with a rope-handle torus, working out coordinates so it avoids overlapping both barrels and sits clear of the chest's back wall in z.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton victim near the trap, placing the skull, spine, and ribcage along an x-axis path with a slight yaw so the body appears to lie naturally in front of the trap frame.

Setting up a world transform combining translation and yaw rotation, then defining a helper that converts local skeleton coordinates into rotated world-space points for the ribs, boxes, and skull.

I'm laying out the skeleton on its back with head toward -x and legs toward +x, placing the skull near the floor and orienting its yaw so the face points toward the viewer.

Now I'm building the rest of the spine: neck vertebrae, ribcage with seven spaced pairs, a sternum rod, continuing vertebral boxes, and a pelvis formed from flared iliac wings plus a sacrum ring, all positioned along the local x-axis.

Next I'm figuring out the leg bones — femurs running from the pelvis down with one straight and one bent at the knee, continuing into the tibia on the bent side.

I'm also checking the overall skeleton placement so it stays within the floor bounds after converting local coordinates to world space with a slight yaw rotation, making sure x and z stay inside the floor limits.

Now I'm checking for overlaps between the coin spill, skull, and trap positions, adjusting the skeleton's center and the trap's z-span so the ribcage doesn't collide with the trap frame edge.

For the arms, I'm positioning the right arm along the body while sprawling the left arm outward with the hand reaching toward the trap, using small merged boxes for the fingers near the trap edge.

I should add a scattered skull or two near the barrels along with a femur and ribs, plus maybe one more small skull on the floor for extra loose detail. Given this will run around 700 lines and I can't run a typechecker, I need to be disciplined about imports -- only importing what's actually used since unused locals and implicit anys will likely be flagged as errors.

I'm listing out the module imports I'll need: Three.js core, geometry merging utilities, the builder, frame, math helpers, path curves, pixel art kit functions, glow, and noise painting. I'll double-check each import is actually referenced later in the code.

Writing placement helper function...

Now I'm setting up flat color conventions for simple parts and sketching out part-construction helpers like the texture box function, including a root joint for the base and type definitions for 3D vectors.

To be safe against exactOptionalPropertyTypes issues, I'll build the options object conditionally, only assigning `rotation` when it's actually provided, and confirm `PartOptions` is exported with a `texture` field and accepts bone as a `Joint` reference.

Now I'm figuring out the color type for parts, using a plain hex string for fill, and planning each wood-textured box tile. I'm starting to design the iron plate texture: a grid of plates with rivets at corners, highlight and shadow edges, and dithered rust patches.

Writing iron tile texture...

Designing the gold tile texture now, laying out a coin-heap pattern with circular coins spaced across the grid.

Still writing coin tile logic...

Designing the lock tile pixel grid...

Still mapping out the pixel grid rows...

Mapping out each row of the icon grid pixel by pixel...

Designing the lock box tile with precise texel sizing so the front face crops exactly one tile, then sketching a simple iron hasp texture with rivets and a keyhole cutout using the iron tile pattern.

For the trap plate tile, I'm laying out a dark steel surface with a 5×5 grid of bolt-hole rims spaced evenly, adding a beveled border for depth, and considering small corner engravings like a skull glyph before settling on keeping the border simple.

I'm adding surface damage detail—2px blood stains with dithering, scratches, corner bolts, and tiny sparkle dots at the gap midpoints between holes. Then I'm working through the UV mapping so the plate texture aligns correctly with the top face of the box geometry, checking that the 44-texel tile matches the 0.88 face size exactly and figuring out which direction u and v run on the top face.

Now I'm confirming the texture orientation: since the grid is symmetric (5×5, centered), the exact direction doesn't actually matter, and the spike centers line up correctly with the hole positions. I'm moving on to designing the stone frame tile—a 32×16 carved block with beveled borders and a small glyph row.

Designing bar tile dimensions...

Still drawing the flame pixel grid...

Checking row widths...

I'm finalizing the flame color palette with deep red, orange, yellow, and white-hot tones, and planning multiple flame variants with different scales and rotations to add visual variety, then setting up the card placement code.

I'm also figuring out glow settings and adding small drifting spark particles above the flame for extra sparkle.

Now I'm detailing the torch head: the cup shape, dark coal/ember box glowing orange inside, and the pitch-soaked rag wrapping made of stacked dark brown boxes with thin wrapping stripes, keeping the palette simple and setting the flame base position relative to the cup's top.

With the ground level set, I'm laying out the torch stand itself: a stone base plinth, a smaller stone tier above it, an iron collar, and then a wooden pole stretching up to head height, while working through texture tiling math to figure out the right texel size so the wood texture scales properly instead of stretching awkwardly across the pole's face.

I settle on a dedicated narrow pole tile with vertical wood grain, rope-wrap bands, and knots at a texel scale that fits cleanly, then move to adding iron reinforcement bands at intervals along the pole and start planning brace rods extending outward from the pole's surface.

Still working out brace geometry...

Now I'm setting the cup base using a lathed shape at the plinth top, sizing it so the rim sits around F+1.41, then adding a small rag-head box tucked inside the cup just above the rim.

Redoing the proportions since the torch was coming out too tall: shortening the pole to 0.85 so the flame tops out near F+1.75 total, and recalculating the cup and flame positions to fit that scale—cup rim at F+1.26, flame base just above it with a height of 0.40. I'm also sizing the pole's tile texture to match (roughly 6×60), and planning small hanging red cloth strips around the collar as drip-pitch rags.

I'll add a small tied banner near the pole top using two boxes, boost the flame and ember glow strength, and reuse a single textured light-pool plane for both torches instead of duplicating it. For floor dressing I'll keep things simple—merged rubble boxes painted with a stone ramp, plus a few flat moss patches near the edges using thin boxes, accepting the blocky look as fitting the pixel style.

I could add a shackle and chain near the skeleton—flattened torus rings lying on the floor at the wrists, with smaller alternating tori forming chain links between them.

Still writing chain link orientation logic...

Now I'm shifting to actually implementing this, starting with imports for the builder, skeleton, framing, math utilities, path/arc helpers, and paint/texture functions I'll need throughout.

Still writing imports and setup...

I'm defining the metadata object for this piece, then setting up constants for texel size and a snapColor helper to quantize colors into a consistent palette for the pixel-art look.

Now I'm writing the floor tile texture generator, which lays out rows of irregular stone blocks with randomized widths and shading, adding moss accents at edges and beveled highlights/shadows per block using hashed noise for variation.

Adding crack details...

Now I'm thinking through a reusable stone tile generator for plinths, with configurable width, height, and row height so I can reuse the texture logic across different blocks.

Writing more tile generators...

Designing the pixel skull-and-crossbones label sprite row by row...

I'm also setting up a puddle alpha texture using an elliptical falloff with some wobble noise for a more organic water shape.

For the pool/torchlight glow texture, I'm computing a radial falloff from center, using a bayer dither pattern to create a soft noisy edge, and mapping intensity to a warm orange-to-yellow color ramp for the glow.

Still writing skull sheet fill logic...

Mapping out facial features now: eye sockets, nose hole, and teeth placement across the cranium and jaw front faces, using coordinate offsets to keep the dark recessed areas distinct from the bone-colored shading.

Then I'm figuring out the box dimensions for the skull parts in pixel scale, confirming cranium size matches an 8×7×8 box, and working out how the cranium should be centered relative to the jaw gap when placed in the final skeleton assembly.

Now I'm working out resting pose: jaw center sits at floor height plus a small offset, cranium sits just above it with mouth closed, and I decide to tilt the whole skull slightly around the z-axis for a more natural propped-up look.

Simplifying further, I'll keep the skull upright with just yaw rotation for ease, and for impaled skulls I'll offset the jaw a bit lower so it hangs open. I'm writing a skull-building function that takes position, yaw, and base height, computing the jaw's offset from the cranium by rotating a local offset vector using the standard Y-axis rotation formulas.

Now I'm sketching a procedural wood-paint function for barrels: it picks a perpendicular "side" vector based on the barrel's axis, then a third vector from the cross product, and uses cell-based painting to color faces differently depending on whether they're a cap or the barrel's curved side.

For caps I'm computing plank seams by quantizing distance along the side vector and darkening every sixth seam line, with brightness varying via a hash function for natural wood grain. For the curved surface I'm computing the angular position around the barrel to create vertical stave seams with darker seam lines and lighter highlighted edges, again using hashed randomness for tonal variation per stave.

I'm adding extra darkening when the normal points inward (interior faces), grime near the plank ends, and moss patches on upward-facing surfaces based on noise thresholds, then applying a final lighting adjustment based on the surface normal's vertical component before returning the picked wood color from the ramp.

Now I'm defining the iron paint with rust patches using noise-based thresholds, similarly for bone, gold, and water materials, then working on the barrel-building function that constructs a lathe profile from a bottom point and axis vector with options for openness and seeding.

Facet orientation should align since both hoops share the same axis and frame, so vertices should line up correctly. For open barrels I'm adding a rim ring hoop at the top to close off the exposed edge.

For the liquid inside an open barrel, I'm adding a thin cylindrical disc painted as water, aimed along the barrel's axis and parented to the base. I'm skipping an extra plank disc since the lathe geometry already covers the top.

I'm considering adding a spigot to the closed barrel: a small iron box cylinder for the tap body plus a wood handle box, placed at the barrel's front near the lower third, keeping it to just a few simple parts. I'll skip extra rope or dent details for now and move on to building the bucket using a lathed staved shell outline.

For the bucket, I'm defining a closed cross-section profile for the staved wood shell, checking that the edges don't cross, then adding two hoop rings lathed at different heights with radii interpolated along the taper. For the handle, I'm sweeping an arc in the XY plane from one side of the rim to the other, rotating 180° about the z-axis so it arcs up and over the rim, using a thin iron-colored four-sided profile parented to the base.
